analyses.video_title: Target's Management Team Deserves Credit for Accelerating Revenue Growth Amid a Challenging Backdrop
analyses.summary:
Parkev credits Target's new management team for reinvigorating growth after a long slump, with net sales up 5.3% in the latest quarter, traffic up nearly 4%, and full-year guidance raised to roughly 5% growth for 2026. He notes sales had been declining from a 2023 peak until early 2026, and trailing revenue now totals about $108 billion, up from around $70 billion in 2017. He praises Target as an early leader in the digital transformation — buy-online-pickup-in-store and drive-up delivery — a playbook Walmart, Home Depot and others later copied.

He frames Target as a more premium retailer that struggled as pinched consumer budgets pushed shoppers toward lower-priced options like Costco and Walmart, which makes the re-acceleration more impressive. On margins, Target historically ran a richer operating margin (around 7-8%, near 9% at the pandemic peak) versus Walmart near 6% and Costco around 3.5%, and management is trying to restore those historical levels. He also walks through inventory turnover as a key retail metric: Target's ~8.2 is normal for it but well below Walmart's ~12 and Costco's ~15, reflecting Target's higher-price, lower-turnover strategy.

On valuation, enthusiasm has lifted Target's forward P/E from about 8 to 16.7. He had rated the stock a buy before the run-up but downgraded to Hold about a month ago (August 21) on valuation. His updated DCF pegs fair value at $93 versus a $160 market price, so he sees considerable downside and reiterates Hold, saying the ~3.3% drop since his last review isn't enough to warrant an upgrade — he'd want a bigger pullback or further fundamental improvement first.

analyses.video_title: Interesting News for Starbucks Stock Investors | SBUX Stock Analysis | BROS Stock
analyses.summary:
Parkev reacts to Starbucks' announcement that it will close roughly 250 stores across the US and Canada, framing it as further evidence of diseconomies of scale — the company has grown so large (40,000+ locations worldwide) that costs are rising faster than sales. He notes this is the second round of closures and expects more, arguing the chain is over-saturated in North America. He points to a decline in operating margin from about 18% in 2017 to roughly 10% today, and return on invested capital falling from above 30% pre-pandemic to just 11-12%, barely covering the cost of capital.

He attributes much of the margin compression to a structural rise in labor costs: a shortage of frontline restaurant workers (affecting McDonald's and Domino's too) and sharply higher minimum wages, especially California's $20+/hour restaurant wage. In his view these are permanent cost shifts Starbucks didn't anticipate, making incremental new locations unprofitable and justifying a strategic shrinking of the footprint.

Parkev credits CEO Brian Niccol — whose track record at Chipotle earns the stock benefit-of-the-doubt — for identifying and acting on the problem, but warns that giving up market share could open the door for Dutch Bros to expand at Starbucks' expense. On valuation he calls a forward P/E of 30 rich for a company in this position and pegs his DCF fair value at $66 versus a market price of $93. He reiterates a Hold rating, saying he loves the brand but wants a considerably better entry point before upgrading to a buy.

Operating margin has slid from about 18% in 2017 to around 10% today
Return on invested capital has fallen from above 30% pre-pandemic to just 11-12%

analyses.video_title: I'm Updating My Outlook on Alphabet Stock
analyses.summary:
Parkev updates his view on Alphabet following management comments at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia technology conference, where the company claimed its AI is 2.7x better than competitors with 80% better price-performance for inferencing. He emphasizes Alphabet's full-stack advantage — custom processing units, its own large language model, and six product lines each with over a billion users — which lets it spread massive AI investment across a huge customer base. Trailing revenue has surpassed $446 billion, the AI business has crossed a $100 billion annual run rate, and the cloud backlog is around $500 billion.

He highlights sharply rising productivity: revenue per employee has nearly doubled over the decade and accelerated since 2024, from about $1.65 million to $2.15 million per employee, with management holding headcount roughly flat. On valuation, the forward P/E of about 22.7 looks reasonable for a company approaching 20% revenue growth with improving margins and strong moats, though he acknowledges the business is riskier than in recent years because of unprecedented, hundreds-of-billions AI spending in a category where Alphabet hasn't yet proven multi-year dominance.

His updated DCF forecasts $7.8 billion of free cash flow this year, turning to negative $32 billion next year as AI capex peaks (he sees peak hyperscaler spending around 2027-2028), then recovering to a large positive figure (~$146 billion) by 2029 as the investments pay off. His DCF fair value is $338 against a $342 market price — fairly valued on DCF, undervalued on forward P/E. Because he ranks Alphabet a 'Hall of Fame' business that he's owned since 2020, he calls it an excellent buying opportunity and reiterates a Buy at his highest conviction level.

stocks.thesis: Full-stack AI advantage, a $100B+ AI run rate, rising revenue-per-employee productivity, and a reasonable forward P/E make this 'Hall of Fame' business slightly underpriced — a high-conviction buy.

analyses.video_title: Is This the Biggest Stock Opportunity in Gaming History?
analyses.summary:
Parkev evaluates Take-Two Interactive ahead of the November launch of GTA 6, whose predecessor GTA 5 has sold over 230 million units since 2013 and remains one of the most successful franchises in history. He argues the excitement is justified but insists on looking at the whole business, not just one game. Revenue has more than quadrupled since 2017 to about $6.7 billion trailing, with management guiding to at least $8 billion this fiscal year, and he expects substantial multi-year growth as GTA 6 rolls out to PC and its online marketplace after the initial launch.

On profitability the picture is mixed: operating margin has been negative since 2024 (though improving), and return on invested capital collapsed as development dragged on. He sees several tailwinds that should make GTA 6 more lucrative than GTA 5 even at similar unit volumes — a shift from physical discs to higher-margin digital sales and much higher average selling prices — and thinks ROIC could climb above 20%, possibly toward 30%, in the first three-to-five years post-launch. R&D as a percent of revenue has jumped into double digits and stayed there.

He cautions that buying Take-Two means betting not just on GTA 6 but on the company's ability to innovate future hits (GTA 7, 8 and others), and the repeated GTA 6 delays don't inspire confidence in that process. Still, the valuation sits at a multi-year low — a forward P/E of 20 with the stock down nearly 20% in 2026 — and his DCF fair value of $202 is right around the $207 market price. He concludes Take-Two is a buying opportunity but explicitly keeps his conviction low given how much value hinges on a single unproven game.

analyses.summary:
Gareth Soloway previews the week ahead with a technical tour of the S&P 500, oil, the 10-year yield, gold, silver, Bitcoin and several individual stocks. He remains short-term bullish on the S&P 500 as long as it holds above his 'neutral zone' line at 7575, and expects a break above 7770 to open a move to an upper trendline around 7800 by early October, with 8,000 possible by mid-October — a 250+ point gain from the current ~7743. He stresses he is long-term bearish (seeing the market eventually 'collapse like a house of cards') but insists the charts are in charge and the breakdown isn't ready yet, noting only a narrow group of large-cap AI names is holding the market up.

On macro cross-assets, he expects crude oil to break down toward $80 over the next few weeks to a month (a bear-flag setup, aided by potential deal overtures ahead of midterms), while the 10-year yield broke out on a bull flag and could tag a high pivot as early as Monday before pulling back to around 5% — a pullback he says would give the stock market confidence to keep rising. He sees gold and silver as range-bound at support (warning of downside to 3,900 gold / $55 silver if support breaks) and Bitcoin holding up after a higher high, expecting a pullback to about 81,000 that must hold as support for another leg up, with 75,500 the next level below.

On individual names: he thinks Micron has upside to fill a gap that aligns with a 786 fib, after which he'd consider a small short; Nvidia is range-bound in a converging wedge with no clear bias but remains the core of the AI trade; and Meta, after a huge run, looks topped with expected downside back to a prior breakout/buyable level. He also cites Apple near all-time highs and Microsoft's strong rebound as part of the small group keeping the market afloat. The video closes with a sponsored promotion for the Rumble Wallet.

analyses.summary:
Parkev examines Novo Nordisk after management guided to only mid-single-digit revenue growth through 2030 and a rise in patients served to over 60 million from about 46.5 million today. Investors expected more given Novo's strong weight-loss franchise, and the muted outlook — plus a looming patent loss on one weight-loss category — has left shares down over 25% year-to-date in 2026. Trailing revenue is about $51.5 billion, more than triple 2017 levels, so investors had grown used to far faster growth.

He walks through the fundamentals: operating margin is lucrative at ~45% but has been volatile between roughly 40% and 47% over the decade, unsettling investors who want to see a stable, rising trajectory. His bigger concern is falling return on invested capital — still strong in absolute terms at ~37% (three-to-four times its cost of capital) but down sharply from the 80-90% range earlier in the decade, raising the question of how far it will fall. Notably, Novo has spent the least on R&D as a percent of revenue among peers Pfizer and Eli Lilly, so overspending isn't the cause — he suspects the effectiveness of those investments. Management has already cut about 12,000 jobs in 2026 and hopes to redirect savings into R&D, and he notes AI could eventually lower drug-development costs industry-wide.

On valuation, Novo trades at a forward P/E of just 11.3, near its cheapest in a long time. He revised his DCF lower after cutting his free-cash-flow expectations and raising his beta assumption to 0.75 to reflect higher forward risk, arriving at a fair value of $64.50 versus a $38.36 market price near the 52-week low — implying about 68% upside over 12-18 months. He keeps Novo rated a buy but lowers his conviction to low as performance keeps disappointing, and states he prefers competitor Eli Lilly, which he owns.

analyses.video_title: Unfortunate News for Oracle Stock Investors | ORCL Stock Analysis
analyses.summary:
Parkev breaks down why Oracle fell nearly 4% after issuing a force majeure notice on its 2.45-gigawatt New Mexico data-center site, 'Project Jupiter,' tied to a startup initiative with OpenAI (the customer) and SoftBank. The notice, reportedly sent to developer/private-credit player Blue Owl Capital, appears aimed at delaying payments if the site fails to come online in 2028. Oracle publicly insisted the project remains on schedule and that such notices are routine, but Parkev argues the sell-off reflects fear of what it could signal about the AI ecosystem's heavy interdependence and circular financing, where companies are simultaneously each other's customers and creditors.

He stresses Oracle is the most leveraged and cash-tenuous of the hyperscalers (citing a KeyBanc analyst), carrying tens of billions in debt with free cash flow expected to stay negative for years, so any adverse change hits its share price harder. A recent positive is that Oracle now collects multi-billion-dollar deposits from customers ordering compute capacity, easing the timing mismatch between huge upfront data-center spending and cash flows that arrive over years. He models negative free cash flow of about $25B in 2026, $37B in 2027, and $32.6B in 2028 (revised less negative after the deposits), with a return to positive cash flow in 2029.

He updated his fair value to $131 versus a $139 market price, so with a margin of safety the stock looks fairly valued on DCF but undervalued on a forward P/E of 12.71 — cheaper than in 2024 despite far more backlog, which he says reflects rising risk as OpenAI's position looks more tenuous (Anthropic's rise, OpenAI's delayed IPO). He concludes Oracle is still a buying opportunity on risk-versus-reward but at low conviction, and flags Micron's earnings after the close on September 30 as the next key AI read.
macro_topics: circular financing in the AI ecosystem

analyses.video_title: Should Investors Buy Costco Stock Instead of Walmart Stock? | COST Stock Analysis WMT Stock Analysis
analyses.summary:
Parkev compares Costco and Walmart, two low-cost retail leaders, to decide which is the better buy at current prices. On revenue, Walmart is more than twice the size ($736 billion trailing versus Costco's $294 billion), but he flags that Walmart does this with over 10,000 locations worldwide while Costco generates nearly half that revenue from fewer than 1,000 stores — which he reads as a long runway for Costco to expand. Costco has historically been conservative about adding locations, maximizing revenue per store, but has been slower than Walmart in e-commerce, where Walmart is the clear leader and has even been gaining share against Amazon by using its store network for fast fulfillment.

He spends time on profitability, noting people are often shocked that both companies earn only about $4 of operating profit per $100 of sales — Walmart at 4.4% and Costco at 3.82% (including membership fees). He stresses retail is a structurally low-margin industry. He then focuses on inventory turnover as the metric that matters most for merchants: Costco's ~15.25 is world-class and well above Walmart's ~12, reflecting Costco's discipline in buying and placing inventory.

On valuation, Costco trades at a forward P/E of 36.3, about a 10% premium to Walmart's 34 — rich multiples for brick-and-mortar retailers that reflect investor respect. His DCF work finds Walmart overvalued (fair value $70 versus a $110 price) while Costco looks more fairly valued (fair value $843 versus a $900 price). Given the choice between the two, he would pick Costco today.
